Thank you, Mr. Chairman. As you know, it is difficult to be required to attend a committee and be obliged to wait for these items over a long period of time, particularly when the committee is sitting. I greatly appreciate your courtesy.
I am one of those who do not make application to any of the ministers for expenditures. I have followed that course consistently, because I believe that there can be no substantial reduction in taxation if we all ask for ever-increasing expenditures while at the same time asking for reductions in taxation.
The St. Lawrence does not flow in your riding.

I do not know the meaning of that statement, but I intend to deal with a body of water which, as far as Saskatchewan is concerned, was at one time the St. Lawrence of that province for the transportation of wheat and other products. On several occasions I have drawn this matter to the minister's attention. It has to do with a lake in the centre of Saskatchewan, namely, Last Mountain lake. One and a half or two years ago I brought this matter to the attention of the minister and he agreed that I had advanced substantial reasons for something being done. Unfortunately, however, nothing has yet been done. I asked for an expenditure to be made in connection with Last Mountain lake and the raising of its level, which I think does not come under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, but, in point of fact, comes
under the Department of Public Works. I ask that this expenditure be made because it will not be a dead expenditure. It will mean an increase in the productivity of the central portion of Saskatchewan. It will mean the preservation of the finest fishing area in the centre of that province, and also the greatest bird sanctuary there. The hon. member for Davenport knows of the necessity for raising the level of this lake. In November 1945 I drew the matter to the attention of the minister, and at page 2668 of Hansard for that year, referring to what I had to say with respect to public works in Saskatchewan, the minister said:
I believe there is something in what he said about the project for Long Lake and the Qu'Appelle river. I have to repeat that there is nothing in these estimates for these works, but they are kept in mind.
Well, Mr. Chairman, while they may have been kept in mind since November 1945, as the months have passed by the level of that lake has gradually gone down, so I again bring this matter to the attention of the minister. I am not going into it at length. As I pointed out before, this would give work to those who are unemployed. It is a productive public work which will return dividends. It has been recommended over the years; it will mean the preservation of a resource the loss of which to Saskatchewan cannot now be estimated, and it would not require any great expenditure of money. I know a survey has been made in this connection, but having regard to the necessity of the preservation of this lake, connected as it is with the Qu'Appelle valley of which a portion comes under his jurisdiction, I ask the minister once more that consideration be given to the preservation of this resource which over the years, as I said to my hon. friend a few moments ago, has performed a function similar to the St. Lawrence.
Many years ago in Saskatchewan marine insurance was in effect on the ships that went up and down Last Mountain lake. It was the first means of transportation in Saskatchewan for wheat produced north of the main line of the C.P.R. It was utilized over the years until about 1910, when railway transportation made it rather too costly. Today the level of the lake is receding. Successive governments have spoken of its value, but the federal government* passes the responsibility to the province, while the province says part of it is navigable waters and within the authority of the dominion; therefore they have no jurisdiction. While the buck is passed back and forth between the two authorities, the lake continues to recede.

Supply-Public Works
I spoke of unemployment, and there is unemployment. We have our share of the 1X8,000 who are unemployed in the dominion today. This would be a particularly helpful piece of work from that point of view. It would assure the preservation of adjacent areas which, if this lake dries up, will no longer be capable of use as farm lands. It would preserve this source of the greatest fishing industry in the centre of Saskatchewan. Once more I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to this matter; and I wish also to ask what he has done since November 1945, when he pointed out to me that no provision was being made at that time because the war had just ended, but that with the ending of the war public works proved to be self-liquidating would receive first consideration from his department.

Before the minister replies I should like to support what the hon. member for Lake Centre has said. I know this lake very well; and, like all lakes in Saskatchewan, it is very important. It is in the central part of the province, and is slowly disappearing. We have all too few lakes which constitute fish preserves, and this lake is particularly important as a tourist attraction. The people of this area are very much concerned about the way this lake is gradually receding. In a matter of only a few years it may be in such condition that it cannot be used for any purpose whatever.

As I recall the discussion in the house two years ago I can admit right- now that when the hon. member spoke of the Last Mountain project and the disappearance of the water from the lake, it was the first time I had heard about it, and I am still quite in the dark. Does the hon. gentleman know if we had a dam there in years gone by?
Yes, a dam was there.

And with the building of the railway the lake lost its use,
I suppose, and the dam disappeared? What would be the suggestion; that we put up a dam there to conserve the level of the lake?
And to permit the conservation of the waters along the Qu'Appelle, and the ultimate diversion of those waters into the lake at periods of the year when the level is low.
It does not come under the P.F.R.A.?
No.
It has no agricultural use?

No. A certain portion comes under P.F.R.A. That has merely to do with the preservation of water for irrigation or local agricultural purposes. This type of project does not and could not come under P.F.R.A.; at least that is the attitude taken by the officials generally with respect to the extensive work that would have to be done.
If there is no navigation on this lake now how could I spend any money there under the statute?
There used to be navigation.

Then my authority would be that these are navigable waters, and we could proceed to conserve the level of the water for navigational purposes? That would be the only way I could justify an estimate for that purpose. The real object would be to keep a natural resource that now exists in that province, so that it will not disappear as time goes on. You have not too much water around there, I suppose, and if one lake should disappear it might have quite an effect on the whole province.
It is the only large lake in the centre of Saskatchewan, the southern portion of which has very few lakes indeed.

This was discussed two years ago, and at the time I admitted my ignorance. Today I am beginning to get some idea of it. I inquired if we had made a survey since 1945, and my deputy is not quite sure but thinks our engineer did go out there.
That is the information I have.

I have not that report here, but after this discussion I shall look into it. I shall not commit my department to these works, but I should like to know about them. I want to find out if the spending of money at that point for conservation purposes would come under the jurisdiction of this department. I am wondering if the outlay would be heavy; because in the past we have entered into some projects which cost millions of dollars.
It would be nothing like that.

That is the reason for the survey. I believe the minister's department has operated in conjunction with the administration of the Prairie Farm
Rehabilitation Act in a general survey. In order to be of assistance, may I point out that

Supply-Public Works
a committee under the chairmanship of Leonard Plaxton of Regina Beach has furnished the various departments with full information with regard' to the matter. Apparently it has not been brought to the attention of the Minister of Public Works.
On November 29. 1945. I went into the matter in greater detail. I would ask that, in the interests of the preservation of a large portion of central Saskatchewan, something be done. The minister has asked, why it should be preserved. Last year the shipment of fish from this lake brought a large income to the farmers adjacent thereto.
Would this be a project in which the provincial and federal governments would join?

There was set up in 1944 and the spring of 1945, a joint committee composed of dominion and provincial officials, who undertook joint public works for the preservation of our natural resources. I believe this project was discussed and was reported upon favourably.
I have told the minister what I said on the earlier occasion, and have given the page number. Perhaps I need not read it at this time. I might add however, that our water fowl are disappearing for lack of sanctuaries. Ducks Unlimited have spent a great deal of money to preserve the habitat and nesting places of our wild life. This is one of them. When I went to Saskatchewan as a boy there were millions of wild ducks, and tens of thousands of wild geese, wild turkeys and cranes. They have disappeared with the drying up of large areas in the province.
This lake, and Redberry lake farther north, are two of the chief sanctuaries in the provinces. That is one reason why something should be done by the federal authorities. I believe the federal government has a responsibility to preserve our wild bird life. There is a convention between the United States and Canada which sets out that everything be done to that end. I advance that also as reason for the minister's giving his best consideration to the preservation of this lake.

I should like to add a few words in support of what has been said by the hon. members for Lake Centre and Wey-burn. I was afraid that when the hon. member for Lake Centre had concluded the minister might jump up and say that this matter comes under the Department of Mines and Resources.
I would have, if it were true.

This project is feasible and should be undertaken. I do not care whether it is done by the minister's department,, under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, under the Department of Mines and Resources, or under a combination of all three. Indeed I believe a combination would be appropriate.
The hon. member would not object to our working with the province?

I am certain the province would be willing to do its share. I would take only one exception to what was said by the hon. member for Lake Centre and my colleague the hon. member for Weyburn. When those who live in the southern part of the province speak about anything in the central portion of that southern part they refer to it as central Saskatchewan. I would draw to the attention of the committee the fact that the centre of Saskatchewan is between Humboldt and Prince Albert.
It is 100 miles north of Prince Albert.

Furthermore we have other bodies of water in Saskatchewan which, in years gone by, I have drawn to the attention of the minister as being worthy of his consideration. I suggest that he ought, not to let those from the dried-out plains of Saskatchewan persuade him that that is the only part of the province. We have in Saskatchewan many bodies of water, and they should not be neglected as Last Mountain lake has been. I suggest that those resources should be cared for. I believe it will be shown in the future that the northern area, which some people do not recognize, will be the basis of some astounding developments.
I note that an amount is to be expended at Waskesiu lake, and that included is a revote of $15,000. This would mean that nothing was spent last year. This year I am pleased to note the amount is $70,000. or $55,000 over last year's amount. If the minister does not make any better progress this year than he did last the vote will be of very little use. Why was the $15,000 not spent last year, and what is the possibility of spending $70,000 this year? I would ask him to remember that we have in northern Saskatchewan rivers and lakes worthy of attention.

Tenders will be asked for this work within a month.
Then, replying to the hon. member for Lake Centre I would say I am not sure that this comes completely under our jurisdiction. However, this matter is of such great interest that, with the assurance given by the hon.
Supply-Public Works

member for Humboldt that the government of Saskatchewan would be willing to study and perhaps to help in this connection, I shall ask our engineer out there to give an estimate. If we have jurisdiction I will try to convince some of my colleagues that this work should be done, especially as the hon. member says there is unemployment in that district. If we have reached the stage where we can start on our post-war projects, this is one in which I would be interested. I am not committing myself, but I am more than interested, and if I go out west in the near future I shall visit that part of the country and see the conditions for myself.

I rise to support the plea of the hon. member for Lake Centre, for this is a part of the western provinces which it became necessary for me to make a fairly substantial survey of in connection with the programme to divert waters from the South Saskatchewan river down the Qu'Appelle valley. If the minister will get in touch with the P.F.R.A. engineers-I believe there are some in the confederation building-he will find that they have plans-at least they have them in Regina, and I presume they sent copies here-of what the P.F.R.A. has in mind to do later on. They propose to divert some water down the Qu'Appelle river from the dam they propose to construct near the elbow, for the purpose of irrigation and for the purpose of providing water for domestic use in the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina.
The minister wondered what place his department would have in that programme. His department would have a part in that programme. The P.F.R.A. would deliver the water. Their plans call for diverting some of that water into Long lake to do what my hon. friend the member for Lake Centre has been asking for, to raise the elevation of Long lake, which years ago was higher than it is today. Boats used to operate on that lake many years ago. It was the only means of transportation for a large volume of materials in the early years. The minister's department would at least have control of the dam at the outlet of the lake, which, if constructed for transportation, too, would have locks in it. I believe that will come, because the P.F.R.A. have already created, close to Long lake, a very large body of water which is called Buffalo Pound lake. They have erected other dams in the valley where they have a series of lakes called generally the Qu'Appelle lakes. I presume that the engineers of P.F.R.A. visualize some years hence a certain amount of transportation in that valley, and if that ever comes, navigation works will be constructed by the department of the minister.

The hon. member for Lake Centre has touched on an important result that would follow from the elevation of Long lake, namely the conservation of wild life, for which that area is very suitable. Raising the level of the lake would have a big influence on all that part of the province from the point of view of both recreation and conservation, and the hon. member for Lake Centre deserves credit for the energy he has put into advocating this project for several sessions now.
I suggest to the minister that if he goes west this summer, as he said a few moments ago he contemplated doing, he take time off to visit Moose Jaw and drive directly north from there by motor through a very nice part of the country. As he motors north he will pass by Buffalo Pound lake, an artificial lake created by the P.F.R.A. engineers, who will go with him and show him their full proposals for the elevation of Long lake level. Once that work is done, it will come under the control of the minister because there will be a navigable lake, which, of course, would be under the jurisdiction of this government. After the minister has made his trip out west, I am sure that he will come back and have something in his estimates for this project. I presume it will have to be in cooperation with the P.F.R.A., because the P.F.R.A. would have to cooperate with the Department of Public Works and integrate their plans. The two go together. I strongly support the recommendation of the hon. member for Lake Centre.

I would draw the minister's attention to the condition of the pier in Pigeon lake. This pier was built by the federal Department of Public Works just before the war, and my information is that because of neglect, unless repairs are soon made to the pier it will be past repairing. Its present condition is due more than anything else to ice conditions, but I am informed by local authorities that those conditions could be overcome. I know the pier myself. Pigeon lake is the main lake south of Edmonton. To thousands of visitors who go there the pier means a great deal. I notice that there is no item in the estimates for the repair of this pier.
Do I understand that the government owns the pier on Pigeon lake?

I do not know that, but I know that the Department of Public Works under the minister's predecessor built the pier just before the war, and so far as I know, no repairs have since been made to it. As a consequence, the pier is in very bad

Supply-Public Works
shape. It cost in the neighbourhood of $15,000, if I remember rightly. Pigeon lake is the main pleasure resort south of Edmonton and the pier is of great use to thousands of visitors.
I will send out an engineer and have a report made. If it is one of our constructions we shall try to keep it in a good state of repair.
Thank you.

Regarding the item for the reconstruction of approach and repairs to the ferry slip at Sidney, I would urge on the minister the necessity of having this work done at the earliest possible opportunity. The amount of traffic coming into that port has been growing considerably every year. It
takes away from the congestion of the facilities at Victoria. The urgency of a work has been emphasized, not only by the Sidney board of trade, but also by the board of trade at Victoria. There are ferry services coming from the state of Washington and from the mainland of British Columbia where it is the shortest sea journey between the island of Vancouver and the mainland of the province. There is communication between Sidney and all the gulf islands, so that there are ships coming in continually with farmers' produce and other supplies. There are hundreds of cars moved over that approach every week during the summer season. For a long time notices have been put up that this approach is unsafe or is to be used only at the owner's risk, owing to the state of disrepair into which it has fallen. The fact that the great terminal of the T.C.A. is only a mile away at Patricia Bay enhances the importance of this particular port. Furthermore, the port services are putting on new and better facilities this year, with the result that the traffic will still be increased, and it is imperative, before the height of the tourist season comes, that something Should be done to repair this particular approach.
I should also like to say that, in order that this work may be of a permanent nature and not have to be repaired every year, it would be most desirable to construct a breakwater just to the south of where the ferry approach now is. That has been given consideration for a number of years, but new suggestions have been made as to the type of breakwater which would make this repair work permanent. I would urge the minister to have this situation reviewed during the coming year, with the idea of seeing whether it would not be possible to erect a breakwater just south of where the ferry approach now is, in order to make permanent the work which he is now putting in, work which is absolutely essential for that growing community.

I should
like to say a few words to the minister with regard to British Columbia generally. Probably the committee has heard quite a lot about that province, but I think it is about time that the public works department and other departments of government got a new appreciation of the way in which British Columbia has been growing in the past ten years and particularly since the war. The growth of the population in that province is acknowledged to be the greatest of any part of Canada. As a matter of fact we have not been in such close contact with the federal government through the medium of the public works department and other public services for as many years as some
Supply-Public Works

of the other provinces. A lot of the work in the construction of piers and breakwaters and that type of thing went on in the maritime provinces, in Ontario and in Quebec many years ago. I say to my hon. friends from the maritimes that I do not begrudge them one dollar that they have received in the past. I do not think they have had enough.
However I wish to point out to the minister that Vancouver island particularly, of which the hon. member for Nanaimo and the hon. member for Victoria have spoken, is one of the places that has developed most rapidly. I could point out to him the necessity of many public works. We are now beyond the item where we are discussing post offices. I am sure that all throughout my riding- and this applies equally to the whole of Vancouver island-the growth of population is such that it is almost a public disgrace what they have to put up with in the line of post office accommodation. So far as breakwaters are concerned, we are in most difficult circumstances.
There is one particular item that I should like to mention. I have discussed it with the minister. I refer to the question of a breakwater for Campbell River. He has heard about that. I would also point out to him the request of the board of trade of Qualicum and the board of trade of Tofino. I am hoping that an item will be placed in the supplementary estimates to give some kind of protection to the wharf at Forde's cove on Hornby island. Actually the difficulty is that every winter they have to move the floats, or else they will wash out.
I notice that there is an item in the estimates for wharf extension at Vananda. There is a revote of $7,500. This is one of the places which has had very rapid development, both in logging and in the operations of the Pioneer Gold Mines. They are carrying on a very large development. The Pioneer Gold Mines have spent $300,000, and their request has been for a more substantial dock over which they could take some of their heavy machinery. They require this improvement to land machinery in order to put in a mill on the property. This year the sum of $8,500 is being appropriated, of which $7,500 is a revote. This will provide, I imagine, a new deck or a few new piles for that dock.
I am hopeful that the requirements of this port will be looked after, so that the residents will have more adequate facilities.

I want to express the
appreciation of some of my constituents in the outlying areas for what has been done with regard to wharf repairs in the past years. One or two new floats have been built. We appreciate the policy of the government in
lMr. G. L. Gibson.]
assisting the people who have located in these out-of-the-way places. We have a number of people whose only means of transportation is by steamer, and they very much appreciate money being spent to assist people in these out-of-the-way places. I think everything possible should be done to encourage these people who are willing to go into the backwoods to make a living. At the same time I wish to express the appreciation of the people for what is being done by the minister for these settlers. During the past year much of the work could not be done because of the shortage of labour and material. We know that your officials did attempt to secure the materials, and that they were partly successful and finally were abie to build the few structures which were erected during the past year.
I want to draw particularly to the minister's attention the urgent necessity for wharves at three or four places. The first I would mention is that of Trail. During recent years there has been an increase in tourist traffic. I think the minister has some knowledge of this. Many tourists come up from the United States by boat and go into the Arrow lakes. One needs to remember that the city of Trail has an annual production of some $60 million, which adds greatly to the revenue of this country. The municipality, the board of trade, the com-merical organizations and all the industries served there are anxious to have some structure erected, so that boats can land in coming up the river. I know a good deal about this, although I am not an engineer. I know the department might hesitate to spend a great deal of money on a structure because of the possibility of developments in the river in the near future, but I suggest that a float could be built which would serve the purpose at Trail for a, few years, and later it could, be towed up the river and into the lake and used as a floating wharf where replacement was necessary at one of the smaller points. I offer the suggestion to the minister.
Then there is a wharf required, in Lardeau, the entrance to the Lardeau valley. Since the early days there has been a very narrow wharf, about ten feet wide. It was erected originally by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and is now in a state of disrepair or decay. Large quantities of lumbering machinery, mining machinery, heavy materials, groceries and so on move over this wharf. They have to be dumped out on this wharf and carted out by hand some distance over the ground to the road. These people who use the wharf are developing this country. I urge the minister and his officials to give consideration to the needs of these people.

Supply-Public Works
I also hope the minister will consider the requirements of the city of Nelson. I do not know what arrangements are being made, but he knows the situation well. There is a demand there for some improvement in the wharf facilities; a new structure is urgently required.
One final plea. I wish to refer to the question of a very small wharf or float that is required, by the small settlement of Dean's Haven. This is a small Veterans Land Act settlement consisting of twenty-five or thirty people. These men have offered to do the work on these wharves for a minimum of expenditure, and. I think the department should be a.s generous as possible to them, seeing that they have gone into the backwoods in an attempt to establish homes for themselves and to develop a small lumber industry. I am interested in noting in the estimates an item of $24,000 for protection work on the Columbia river. Where is that, work to be done?

Can the minister say what, progress has been made in implementing the report of the joint engineers on the Okanagan flood control? I am not going to make a speech on the subject, although there is plenty of material. The minister will recall that a joint committee of engineers of the dominion and provincial governments was set up in 1943 and duly reported, making its recommendations. This came about after public meetings and public hearings and after a considerable amount, of damage had been done to 100 miles of the lower Okanagan valley as a consequence of the flooding of Okanagan lake. The dominion government is interested in the matter because of the navigability of the water and because, for many years it has operated the control work at the south end of the lake. That control work is inadequate for its purpose, and the tortuous course of the Okanagan river makes it impossible for the flood water to be carried off safely. The municipalities and everyone in the district were extremely interested when this joint committee was set up, but now we want to know what progress will be made with the acceptance or otherwise of the recommendations in the report. I hope the minister will be able to tell me that, meetings will be held between him and the provincial government for the purpose of deciding what will be done.

In 1943 a joint committee or commission did make a report. At the time I looked over the report, and it is quite a project, involving a considerable amount. The last I heard was that they want us to appoint, without committing the government, someone from the department or the government to continue discussions on the feasibility of an agreement to be made between the British Columbia government and these people. I understand that we shall be sending our representative the moment we hear from them. As a matter of fact, the date was fixed, but the three parties could no come together at the same time. I has-been fixed now for September of this year when the representatives of the three sides will meet.

Will the minister be good enough to follow this matter up? It is a question affecting a difficulty that has been apparent for many years, and at last, when the committee reports that there is something tangible to lay hold of, I would ask the minister to see to it that, the representative of the dominion meets with the province for the purpose of coming to a conclusion.
I will attend to that myself.
Has the minister anything to say with regard to the completion of the road between Jasper and Prince George?
That comes under the Department of Mines and Resources.
Can the minister answer the question I asked him?

My officials will take a note of every request made by the hon. gentlemen. I did not get every name he mentioned, but the moment a request is made our engineers make a note of it. They will look into the different projects and report upon the necessity for those that are new; and, as regards maintenance or repairs, we shall see that they are done.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing item 344. Shall the item carry?

I am not opposed to this item. I am certainly not. opposed to the appropriation indicated on page 212 of the estimates of $50,000 for the purchase of works of art. It is possible that it should be larger than that. I believe, however, that when public money is being expended this house should know exactly for what purpose it is to be used. I sincerely hope that the emphasis is being placed on the purchase of works of art produced by Canadians. Our artists need encouragement and there are Canadian artists of considerable note. As a matter of fact, I need only draw the house's attention to the picture in the rotunda of the parliament buildings, a picture painted by Mr. Forbes, a Canadian, to illustrate the fact that we have artists of more than average note in this country. Canadian artists do not need and have never needed to take second place to anyone. Our artists ought to be encouraged and, I believe they are being encouraged. I am not suggesting for a moment that those who operate the national gallery have not considered that. They have different projects and receive requests; and when they come to some decision, or decide that a federal project would be useful at the proper time, we work on the details of the specifications for the project.

I would direct the minister's attention to pages 210 and 211 of the details. We find there that we have already passed about $600,000 or $700,000 for such things as temporary assistance. I was talking about that item last night.
Then there is reference to commissions, whatever they are, to the extent of 8300,000 or $400,000. I should like to know what those commissions are.

I understand that those commissions are paid to the telegraph or telephone operators we have throughout the country on government-owned lines. They are not paid monthly or weekly rates, but are paid according to the amount of business going through the offices or probably a percentage of collections made.

The minister has
said that item 307 deals with dredging for Ontario and Quebec, and referred to dredging on lake Ontario. This involves an expenditure of about $376,000, and I should like to know something about it.

Mr. Chairman, so far
as I can see, the post office service has improved. I do not know who deserves credit for it, but perhaps it should go to the minister, as head of the department. I do not hear any complaints any more in my own city of Toronto, and I presume that the service has improved generally throughout the country.
Come up to my riding.

I am speaking of a city riding. I would ask the minister if the department has made any decision yet as to reducing the air mail postage rate. I found everywhere in the western states when I was there last fall that when I sent letters back to Canada the air mail rate was five cents, whereas in Canada it is seven cents.
It was my intention to say a few words about the balance sheet of the department.
Will the minister explain the $11,000,000 surplus?

Our total gross revenue in 1945-46 was $83,785,000, as against $86,400,000 in 1946-47. The revenue was as follows: postage stamps, cards, et cetera, sold, $52,000,000 in 1945-46 and $55,000,000 in 194647; postage paid in cash, 1945-46, $23,000,000; 1946-47, $24,000,000; deductions from revenue, postmasters' remuneration, commissions and allowance. 1945-46, $10,211,000; 1946-47, $10,427,000; discount to stamp vendors, special 83166-306
delivery compensation, transit charges, et cetera, 1945-46, $4,900,000; 1946-47, $2,995,000. So that the net revenue in 1945-46 was $68,635,000 and in 1946-47, $72,978,000.
Now for the expenditures. In 1945-46 they totalled 857.729,000; 1946-47, $64,213,000. This increase is due to the fact that we are paying more to the employees and also we have a few more employees. We have established new post offices and rural mail routes and are paying quite a sum more on rural mail contracts. We have also established letter carriers in different cities where we did not have them last year.
The net surplus in 1945-46 was $10,905,000, and in 1946-47, $8,765,000.
Nearly $2,000,000 'difference?

Yes, because our expenses have increased. The net surplus after adjustments, was $12,552,000 in 1945-46, and $10,400,000 in 1946-47. The difference is because our expenses have increased. We have adjustments covering the franking privilege, building rental and so forth, and we put that in at $4,728,000 in 1945-46 and $4,750,000 in 1946-47.
As was said on the public works estimates, these figures do not show a profit or loss at all. They simply show an operating surplus over expenses. We do not pay for the buildings, not even for their maintenance. It is just an operating surplus. Some people ask why we should not have a balance sheet just as a company would have; but it must be remembered that we are only one department of the government, and our balance sheet, our profit and loss if you will, so far as the post office is concerned, becomes a part of the government's budget.
The postage value of franked provincial government documents, ballot boxes and keys, customs notices and so forth, was put at $162,875 in 1945-46, and in 1946-47 we are putting it at $150,000. The estimated expense of operating the post office savings bank, wffiich we operate without any charge whatsoever, was S260.S92 in 1945-46, and in 1946-47 we are estimating it at $290,991.
The estimated cost of the free conveyance of newspapers in a forty-mile area was $30,000 in 1945-46 and the same in 1946-47.
The rental value of post office space in government-owned and rented buildings was $3,535,815 in 1945-46 and $3,586,000 in 1946-47.
The net surplus, after adjustments, was $12,552,000 in 1945-46 and $10,400,000 in 1946-47.

I have a few questions I should like to ask the minister specifically regarding the postal district of Moose Jaw. On April 16, in the "Post Office Weekly Bulletin" this announcement was made by the deputy postmaster general:
From April 1, 1947, the position of district director has been discontinued.
Operating and secretarial features will be taken care of by a postmaster; district office functions relating to services and investigations will be carried on by the district post office inspector.
There are two exceptions to the above arrangement, namely. Moose Jaw and Charlottetown. The work of the Moose Jaw district will be under the jurisdiction of the district post office inspector at Calgary, but for the time being the former district director at Moose Jaw will act on behalf of the district inspector at Calgary.
I do not need to tell the minister that the people of Moose Jaw are perturbed by this announcement. They are afraid that they will lose a good many of the staff at the Moose Jaw post office to some other city. This is what the mayor had to say a few days ago in a letter to me:
In my opinion the technique which is being used is not difficult to recognize; and while the head office is to be at Calgary, I would wager that within a year the present form of administration will turn up in Regina.
I should like the minister to make some statement on that fear. In a letter dated April 18, 1947, the mayor of Moose Jaw said:
I have information which, if true, appears to indicate that Moose Jaw district is being discriminated against, for it has been stated to me

Supply-Post Office Department
that of the fifteen districts in this country which have been established, Moose Jaw is the only one to be affected by this proposed and suggested "stream-lining" of the post office districts.
I have one other statement I should like to read, which appeared in the Moose Jaw Times-Herald on April 17 and which, I think, sums up the situation very well:
The announcement from Ottawa has come as a rude shock.
The Moose Jaw postal district, with headquarters at Moose Jaw, was created in 1907 in order to overcome problems created by the fastgrowing population in southern (Saskatchewan and the creation of many new towns as railway lines were built. Prior to the establishment of the Moose Jaw district, the territory between Winnipeg and Calgary, close to 1,000 miles wide and 350 miles in depth, was administered and supervised from Calgary and Winnipeg. This was found to be uneconomical and inefficient.
The reorganization, which has been announced in what appears to be a surreptitious manner, restores the condition of affairs which existed up to 1907.
Those who have engineered the reorganization appear to have been so illogical in their decision that it looks ridiculous. To explain it on the ground of efficiency and for economical reasons is not sound reasoning. It is impracticable and has been proved to be so.
I could go on, but I will not. I have a series of questions that I should like to ask the minister to clear this matter up. Perhaps before I ask these questions, the minister will make a statement. The fact is that in Moose Jaw there have been 625 small rural post offices which have been supervised from that point. Now apparently they are to be supervised from Calgary.
There is nothing wrong with that.

We think there is.
Before I ask my questions perhaps the minister would make a general statement. If it is satisfactory I might not have to ask my questions. If he can clear the matter up I should like him to do so.

We are trying to better the system all over Canada. There is one thing that sometimes creates difficulty. It is the fact that provinces are jealous of their districts, but we are a national department and cannot go according to provinces except in a province like Prince Edward Island which is an island, and we cannot have it administered by somebody who lives outside that island. I shall give the committee an example. The districts are created generally according to a central city. Take the district of Montreal. The district of Montreal goes quite far into Ontario toward Toronto, because Montreal is near the 83166-306J
boundary of Ontario, and the officers have to live in Montreal.
Some time ago we had a little difficulty because we used to have a district starting in Quebec and going as far as Cochrane in Ontario. We thought it was too far for our officers to travel and do a good day's work. They had to work during a part of the night in order to get through, so we cut it and gave North Bay that part of northern Quebec, which is much nearer to North Bay than it is to Quebec. Previously we had a district director in each of fifteen districts, and in each of those cities he was also postmaster and supervisor of the surrounding district. We thought it would provide a better service if we had a district post office inspector besides the postmaster in these large cities. It is enough for a man to be postmaster in Montreal or Toronto, and so we appointed district post office inspectors. Consequently we have two men doing today the work that used to be done by one man, the object being that the work shall be expedited. It was too much for one man.
That is not the case in Moose Jaw.
Moose Jaw and Calgary are not so far apart.
Oh, they are quite a distance.

Well, there are great distances in the western provinces, and we do not want to discriminate against Moose Jaw at all, but it was far more convenient for that district to be administered from Calgary than from Moose Jaw. We had many protests, but it does not change a single man. The man who used to be the district director of Moose Jaw is the postmaster of Moose Jaw, and will stay there, but the man we appointed for that district will live in Calgary instead of Moose Jaw. If we had put it in Moose Jaw he would have had to live there.
Is the minister saying that the present staff in Moose Jaw will not be reduced by that change?
Not one man will be changed.
There will be no change in the future.

I will tell the hon. gentleman more than that. We decided that before making the appointment we would see the people and have a discussion with them. The district might be known as Calgary-Moose Jaw or something like that.

Supply-Post Office Department
We want to arrive at a goodcompromise and therefore we have not yet made the appointment.

The people of Moose Jaw are a little afraid that this appointment, having been made on a temporary basis, will be put in Calgary for a year, and then slipped back to Regina. Is there any possibility of that?
There is no possibility at all. It will not be done, because Regina would not be the proper place.
I thank the minister. Will he tell me what economies are being effected by having it in Calgary instead of Moose Jaw?

The department will probably save between $2,000 and $3,000 in travelling expenses through the district post office director living in Calgary instead of Moose Jaw. He would have to do more travelling if he lived at Moose Jaw. Moreover, from what I am told, Moose Jaw is a smaller city than Calgary.
Before making this permanent, will the minister give the matter further consideration as to leaving it in Moose Jaw?

I have
promised some of my colleagues here, inter alios the bon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), to consider the matter and I am awaiting the return of the deputy minister from France. He is in Paris at the meeting of the international postal union. We will discuss it further and no one will be taken by surprise.

I have one or two observations to make on this. I wish to commend the minister for having relieved the old district director from the responsibility of being also postmaster. I think it was an almost intolerable combination. I should like to ask whether the former district director, who is now to be district inspector, will be in any way penalized as far as salary is concerned.
They will not be penalized in the matter of salary. The salary might even be increased.

It is observed that the Calgary district, for example, is to be enlarged by the inclusion of the Moose Jaw district. Since these districts were before so greatly enlarged, I think the department would be well advised to consider the establishment of additional postal districts in Canada. I believe that fifteen are altogether too few to enable these men to render the type of service which I am sure they are willing to give.

I wish to bring up a point which perhaps would properly come up under item 265; but, inasmuch as it is the only point I am raising tonight, perhaps I may be allowed to discuss it now. I am referring to the new air route now established between Yancouver and Prince Rupert. I will take it for granted that Canadian Pacific Air Lines will get an air mail contract. I will not argue about it because I think it is the only sensible thing to do. It has a land plane as far as Sandspit on the Queen Charlotte islands and from Sandspit to Prince Rupert transportation is by amphibious craft. In considering an air mail contract with the Canadian Pacific Air Lines, I wish the minister would do all he can to have that plane call at the little village of Massett at the north end of the Queen Charlotte islands. They liave a boat only once every ten days and they cannot reply to mail by the same boat, so that sometimes it is twenty days before a letter can be answered and the matter involved squared away. It would not necessitate the plane calling every day. If it could call every two or three days I think the people would be well satisfied, and that would help in the building up of that little community. It would help to make it more prosperous if it were enabled to maintain air communication with the outside.

I wish to reply to the hon. gentleman's statement because it is important. In the department we are air-minded to a reasonable extent, because it costs a good deal of money. We know that in the future we shall use planes more and more for the carriage of mail; and in a country like Canada, which is so vast, the reduction of distances is certainly a very good objective. Between Vancouver and Prince Rupert, Canadian Pacific Air Lines have asked for a licence, which has been granted, effective on June 15, 1947. Of course they are asking for an air mail contract. The post office has often been looked upon by aviation companies as a Santa Claus and it has been a Santa Claus for many of them; but we believe that a contract should be granted to Canadian Pacific Air Lines for this flight. It will go to Prince Rupert and stop at Port Hardy and Sandspit. The hon. member for Skeena has already discussed with me the possibility of the plane stopping at Massett. His reason seems to be a very good one. If it is possible to do that, we shall do so. I may say that this is going to cost approximately $112,680 a year on the basis of thirty cents a mile. There will be a deficit, of course; but we think that far distant points, such as Prince Rupert, should har e faster service than

Supply-Post Office Department
is possible by boat or train. We have also granted a contract to the Canadian Pacific Air Lines for Flin Flon, Port Dauphin and Winnipeg. This is going to cost $82,000. For quite a long time we have been pressed for another contract in the Okanagan valley between Vancouver, Castleaen, Penticton and Kimberley. We are considering that. It is costly, but we will do it if we possibly can.

Can the minister tell me if letter carrier service is soon to be instituted in Swift Current? I have a letter from the assistant district director indicating that a re-survey was made in that week of May 5-10, or some time in there. He advised me that a report of that survey would be made immediately to the Post Office Department at Ottawa for its consideration. Has consideration been given to that report, and what has become of it?
What is the population?
About seven thousand.

In view of the statement made by the Postmaster General to the effect that the department was air-minded, may I ask if the department keeps separate records in respect of the sale of air mail stamps? I would judge from the minister's shake of the head that the answer is no. If they had done so, I feel reasonably sure that the extreme eastern provinces and the extreme western ones would show that they were carrying a large proportion of the sales. I make that statement because of the large amount, in comparison with the other provinces, which is paid in connection with long distance telephone calls. A large number on the extreme east coast-and the same thing applies to the west coast-find it necessary to telephone to central Canada in regard to business and general matters. The same situation does not exist to the same extent in so far as the central provinces are concerned.
Oh, yes.

Not to the same extent, I said. I think the same applies with respect to the air mail service. I bring this matter to the attention of the Postmaster General for this reason. In the maritimes and in the extreme west, if we want a special delivery letter to be delivered, we are obliged to put on a four-cent stamp and a ten-cent stamp. But that is not of very much use to us for a special delivery letter. We always send it by air mail, and it costs us seventeen cents as against fourteen cents for the regular mail in the central provinces. Iam suggesting that consideration be given to a special delivery stamp, air mail, at twelve cents; that is seven cents plus five cents. Of course that privilege would be enjoyed by all sections of Canada, but it would benefit the east and the west to a

Supply-Post Office Department
greater extent than it would benefit central Canada. I am offering that as a constructive thought for the Postmaster General to take into consideration for the future.
I will take note of what the hon. member says.

Has the reorganization which the Postmaster General intimated was taking place extended to the rural post offices? I am not talking about the carriers. Is there an extension of the policy to have more post offices on the staff basis; that is, the postmaster and his assistant being employees of the Post Office Department, instead of having the work let out on a contract basis? If so, what is the minimum revenue requirement before a post office may be placed on a staff basis. Then I have one other question to ask.

The answer is yes; and the minimum requirement has been fixed at $40,000, but we hope to be able to reduce it. That requirement was put on during the war years; but now that the war is over, we hope to be able to lower it, and* it is our intention to have more staff offices as soon as they bring in enough revenue.
That would give a rural postmaster an opportunity of being promoted to a senior station, would it?
Yes.
The minister referred to the extension of the letter carrier service, and the taking on of more employees. Is there any age limit beyond which you do not accept employees?

Not for the returned men, but for the others we are bound by the limit imposed by the civil service commission, which is thirty-five years of age. That does not apply to returned men; even if they are over thirty-five we take them.

And that applies to
employees inside the post office, as well as to letter carriers?
Yes, they come under the civil service commission, like any other employee on the staff here in Ottawa or any other large city.

The Postmaster General said it was the desire of his department to create more staff offices now that the war is over, and that they were considering lowering the requirement, by which I suppose he means the income of an office. In the town of Collingwood, which is in the riding I represent, we have almost the revenue necessary for the establishment of a letter carrier service.
[Mr. Isnor.l
How are your sidewalks?

About the finest one will find anywhere in Canada, and that goes for everything else in the town of Collingwood. At the present time I believe the revenue of that post office is approximately $27,000. I understand that it would require the services of eight returned men to carry on such a service. Eight men working eight hours a day would mean a total number of hours much less than that spent by the householders of that city who have to go to the post office at least once a day for their mail. In most oases it is the women who collect the mail. It has been brought to my attention repeatedly that most of these women cannot afford maids; they have several children in the family, and it means the mother must prepare the children each day, take them to the post office and bring them home again. This means at least two hours lost by most of the women in Collingwood, which would mean thousands of hours of work lost every week. So I suggest that eight men working eight hours a day delivering mail actually would bring about a tremendous saving in work hours and, therefore, an actual saving of money in that community. I should like the Postmaster General to give his assurance that he will reconsider the question of mail delivery in the town of Collingwood. I understand that the requirement for such carrier delivery is an annual revenue of $30,000, and I believe the annual revenue at Collingwood is about $27,000. I believe this matter has been brought to the attention of the hon. gentleman on other occasions, and I think it deserves his serious consideration.

Of course, if
many questions are asked about particular places I shall be unable to answer them immediately, but it is my intention to do what I did last year and read over all these questions when we are through and see if we can satisfy hon. members. I believe it is not considered a good thing for a minister to boast too much about his own department, but as much as possible we try to say yes when we are asked to do something. We are giving a service; we are glad to give it, and we are always sorry to have to say no. In Collingwood last year the revenue was $34,226, which is not very far from the requirement of $40,000. I understand that the population is 5,600; but hon. members must take into account that if we do not have 2,000 points of call it is not economical tc give letter carrier service. It takes at least four letter carriers for a small town where there are 2,000 points of call, with a

Supply

Post Office Department
fifth carrier for relief and to help the others. If there are fewer points of call it is a difficult matter to organize economically. Collingwood is not very far from the requirement, however, and I shall give serious consideration to the hon. gentleman's request.

In view of the fairly good
showing of the Post Office Department in its surplus of receipts over expenditures during the last few years, I wonder if the minister and the government have given consideration to reducing the postal rate on ordinary mail from four cents to three cents.

I have quite
a good answer to that question. This surplus is a tax, as a matter of fact. A tax of one cent was put on in 1931, and a tax of another cent was added in 1943, so that in the four cents there is a tax of two cents. It is not in my power today to reduce that tax; that is a matter which must be dealt with in the budget. I may tell the hon. member, however, that I do not believe it would be a good move to go back to the three cent and two cent rates, because expenses today are much higher than they were before the war. I do not want to say anything against our neighbours in the United States, but immediately after the war they reduced their rate from four cents to three cents for the forward letter and from three cents to two cents for the drop letter, that is, the letter which is delivered in the same city. At the same time they increased the salaries of their postal employees; and today they have a deficit of $492,000,000. It does not take long to create a deficit if you reduce your receipts. Hon. members should remember that we sold $55,000,000 worth of stamps last year. To reduce the rate by one cent on both drop and forward letters would mean a loss in revenue of $11,000,000, and we would be immediately in the red.

What would be the
result if you reduced the air mail rate to five cents?

The air mail rate in the United States was reduced from eight cents to five cents. At the present time a committee of the senate and house of representatives are studying the question of raising the air mail rate from five cents to six or seven cents. We do not know yet what will happen. The President has sent a message to congress asking that it be studied, with a view to recovering part of their deficit.

The minister spoke about the desire of the post office to serve. Certainly in my experience may I say I have had nothing but the most courteous consideration of any requests I have made. I have never gone as high as the minister himself, but I have always had the greatest courtesy from the officials.
Sometimes it is better to go to the officials. They can give more direct answers.

There was one point the minister mentioned with respect to bonuses which interested us a year ago when they were authorized. If I got the figures correctly the minister mentioned, first of all, 374 cases where no previous allowance had been made and on which there was an increase of 21-8 per cent. Then he gave a list of 260 on which there had already been a considerable allowance and, as I understood him, the allowance there was just as great as in respect of those which had had no previous allowance. On the face of it, that would appear strange, and I wonder if the minister would explain it?

These last ones, where there were supplementary payments, were the worst. Those were contracts which had been awarded on tenders first. Of course tenders are not at a set rate. Those 260 were the ones which were lowest and had already been adjusted. But, even after the adjustments, when we passed the law which allowed the readjustment of some of these contracts we found that these contracts had to be given another supplement which would bring them to about the same as those which had not been adjusted before. Those which were adjusted twice received, as a second adjustment, almost as much as those which were adjusted only once. That is because they were lower than the first ones. After they had been adjusted, the high cost of living forced us to adjust them a second time. But the percentage of adjustments, including the two adjustments in the second group and the one adjustment in the first, amounted to about the same thing.
Were the adjustments pretty much on a level? Were they more or less on the same percentage basis? There was not much variation?

No, because the instruction was given to Mr. Herring, the officer in charge, who knows the department very well, to adjust them according to the prevailing rate, which would be the reasonable rate in the area. They were adjusted when they were found to be too low.

What is the policy of the department with regard to the building of new

Supply-Post Office Department
post offices, particularly in rural areas? My understanding is that during the war no new post offices were built where the revenue did not exceed $10,000. Does that policy still hold?

My colleague the Minister of Public Works has complained that I made many requests for new post offices. I admit that for six or seven years- perhaps I should say five or six years-post offices were not built except where they were absolutely necessary. Those were war years. We hope next year to be able to build quite a number. I have said we would build them where the revenues were $10,000 or more, and if it were possible to build them where revenues were lower we would do so with pleasure. There may be a few exceptions here and there, but the fact is that we would be building quite a. number. I would not say the number at this time.
We could leave that off until after the elections, could we not?

Perhaps it would be a good thing, from the point of view of the treasury, but you may be sure that if we could do it this year we would. Doing it next year or the year after will certainly bring it nearer an election; but it would not be for that purpose at all. There will not be any distinction as between constituencies which elect good Liberals, good C.C.F.'ers or good Progressive Conservatives.

I hope what the minister has said does not apply to extensions of post offices already existing. I have one in mind at Steinbach, Manitoba, where they have been after the department for years t'o have their post office enlarged. The building is much too small for the present population. There they have been met with the objection that the department would not make expenditures where revenues were not over $10,000. During the war the revenue in that post office was slightly below this amount. The people in the district claim that they can scarcely get over that amount with the accommodation they have. At the present time I understand that most of the business houses are doing their business directly with Winnipeg by means of the buses which go to that city daily. They buy large quantities of stamps in the city before coming to the town, and in this way the department is losing revenue. The revenue of the post office is not increasing, and yet, since the beginning of the war, the population has almost doubled. I would ask the minister to look into this matter particularly.
We will.

In connection with rural mails, let us suppose there are two routes of twenty miles each, with fifty stops on one and one hundred on the other; how does the department arrive at payment on a mileage basis as. between those two routes?

When the routes are established we ask for tenders. The gentleman who tenders will know the amount at which he should place his tender in order to make a fair living. If a tender is too high we reserve the right to ask for new tenders. That has happened often. If it is a renewal of contract and we pay a supplement we keep in mind that the man who served one hundred boxes should be paid more than the man who served fifty.
But the minister says the payment is at a certain amount per mile. Let up suppose the payment is on that basis, but there are fifty people an one route and one hundred on the other.

We do not pay the contractors by the mile. We ask for tenders, and they tender for a certain amount for the full route. If we adjust such a contract, of course we will adjust it and give a little more to the man who serves one hundred than to the man who serves only fifty
Has there been any general reduction in the hours worked by the employees of the department?
No, they work forty-four hours a week.
Provision is made for 1,020 additional employees over last year. Is that on account of the normal expansion of the service?

Yes, there has been quite an increase in post office business. For example, the sale of monesr orders and postal notes last year amounted to $498,000,000, and this year, $611,000,000, a record figure. That is only one illustration of how business has increased. The restoration of two deliveries a day has also necessitated employing a great many more letter carriers in the cities.
The department is budgeting for an increase of $180,000 for temporary help. I suppose the same explanation would apply there, an anticipated expansion of business?

I could give details of the number of extra employees taken on, especially at Christmas, if the hon. member wanted them. I have here some figures as
