The temporary employees are, I understand, more or less seasonal employees. Can it be anticipated that they will become permanent?

A certain number of temporary employees are employed full time the year round. If they succeed in passing an examination and are returned men they get the preference in appointment. If not, they have to wait until their turn on the eligible list is reached. At Christmas we take temporary employees on by the thousands. More than 5,000 temporary employees are taken on at Toronto for the Christmas rush.
How long has a temporary employee to serve in the department before he is eligible for permanent employment?

At least one year, but during, the war we took on a lot of temporary employees who have now served for two, three, four and five years. I do not like it when we have to tell them that we have to replace them by the veterans, but that is the law and we have to comply with it.

When the minister asked for an increase of $2,387,714 in his estimate, is that simply to provide for the normal expansion of service such as the minister indicated by the monthly increases which he gave a moment ago of post office business?
Yes.
As to the bonus for rural mail carriers, are the carriers still eligible to apply for the bonus, or has that all been completed?
It is not completed. We have applications coming in all the time.
And you are still giving consideration to it?
Yes. We have one year during which we may increase their compensation.

I realize that the minister and his officials are giving careful consideration to the provision of a letter carrier delivery for Port Alberni. I am sure the minister appreciates that Port Alberni is becoming one of our most important cities in Canada. It is the third largest lumber exporter in the country, a fact which is not very well known. I am sure the minister will recall having visited there while he was minister of fisheries, and I can assure him that he has many good friends there who still remember him very kindly. That city has had the most phenomenal growth of any city in Canada. I should like the hon. member for Davenport to visit us. I am sure it would add greatly to his knowledge.
I have it on my itinerary.

I sincerely hope that the hon. member can visit us. We have a population of 10,000 and a substantial postal revenue. Unfortunately we are not in the position of some eastern towns. In the good old days when there was a surplus of cement your towns in the east borrowed money and laid sidewalks. Port Alberni is prosperous and is prepared to lay sidewalks but it cannot get any cement. The city council and the board of trade there are anxious to cooperate with the minister, but everybody in that 10.000 population has to crowd into the small post office every evening for the once-a-day distribution of mail, and this creates an almost impossible situation, necessitating the provision of a letter carrier service in the town. That would save the department a large investment in a post office building, which is urgently needed, but which, I appreciate, is difficult to have built at the present time. I and the minister's friends would appreciate it very much if a letter carrier service could be provided for Port Alberni this year.

I might inform the hon. member that the post office revenue at Port Alberni last year was 841,234. I know the town well. I have been there, and it does not need many more industries to have sidewalks built of lumber for the whole town if cement cannot be obtained.

Supply-Post Office Department

A few moments ago the minister mentioned the postal rate in the United States. Since the United States postal rate has been reduced to three cents, the people there mail their letters here for three cents and when they are delivered the people in Canada have to pay an extra two cents on them.
No.
They have been doing that.

According to the postal convention, a letter posted in the United States at the United States postal rate, which is three cents today, is delivered anywhere in Canada at that rate, without another cent being asked for.
Extra postage has been demanded on post cards.
Extra postage might be required if the letter was much overweight, but our postal convention requires us to deliver United States letters to Canada at the prevailing rate in the United States.
Postcards have been sent over here and the recipients have had to pay extra on them. It may have been a mistake on the part of the post office.
Those were postcards?
Yes.

They had to put one cent on them. The postcard is printed matter, but it becomes a letter when there is writing on it and we have to collect the one cent here which we account for to the United States. They tax it and we have to collect it and account for it. It is not the Canadian postal authorities who tax; it is the United States authorities. When they get these postcards they tax them, and we have to collect the tax when we deliver the postcard and account for the one cent.
That may be the reason.
Yes.
I am glad to have the minister's explanation. It is, of course, a Canadian stamp that is put on it here.
We have to account for it.

The post office workers throughout Canada asked the department some time ago to restrict or limit the size of envelopes. They object to the wee ones that are sent out by some people. They say it slows up their work. Has anything been done with regard to that?

We have a letter which we call "Canada air mail" which is used for air mail. One of these days we shall have to emphasize the regulations in so far as light paper for air mail letters is concerned. We have come to the point where, instead of sending fifty air mail letters to the pound, we do not have more than thirty, thirty-one or thirty-two letters to the pound.

It was the size of the envelopes that the workers were objecting to because there were so many small ones going through. When the minister was talking about the rural mail contractors he did not say whether any who applied for bonuses were refused. Have any been refused?
Oh, yes.
Does the minister know how many?
If Mr. Herring were here he would be able to give us the figure, I suppose. There were requests that were absolutely unreasonable and of course they were refused.
Will the minister tell the committee what revenue was received from the sale of stamps to collectors?
To philatelists; it is extraordinary. The Graham Bell stamps brought in $125,000 before they were issued. The money was sent in by philatelists all over the world who wanted to have that stamp.
It is almost a clear profit.

The total
amount for the year is over $300,000.
That would be almost a clear profit.
Well, it is.
Velvet.

"Velvet," the hon. member for Davenport says. The minister has had representations from Peterborough in regard to the crowded post office there and the conditions which exist in that building. After the mail comes in, the sorters have almost to get out of the building because there is no room for them to work. What is the minister doing about the matter?
I admit that the situation there is very bad. That is one of the post offices that we have considered.

The minister mentioned a moment ago that the Bell telephone stamp brought in about $300,000.

Supply-Post Office Department
Who paid for the cost of printing that stamp, the Post Office Department
The department.
-or the Public Works Department.

The department. The public works department do not print our papers; they do not print our stamps. They furnish us with good quarters whenever they can, with the buildings; and they maintain the buildings; we pay for the bags; we pay for the printing and everything.
Does the public works department pay for the coal, water and light?
Yes; that is included in the maintenance of the building.

When the minister was speaking a while ago he spoke about the tremendous deficit of $492 million in the United States post office department as compared with our own. I wonder whether the United States post office department conducts its business as we do ours in Canada. It seems to me that the Post Office Department is one of those departments which are owned by the government and operated as a monopoly. It is a department which is sometimes used as an illustration of socialism, state ownership. Yet, since the war started, we have raised the price of the stamps one cent. During the first great war we raised the price one cent.
Not since the war, during the war.
About 1941.

During the first great war we put on the first extra cent, which brought us from two cents to three cents. Then in 1941. I believe, another cent was put on, which brought it up to four cents. Despite all these increases, our department has had a surplus of something like $11 million.
Two years ago; this year it is $8 million.

Despite these surpluses, the department does not pay any of its overhead expenses. Whoever heard of a business being conducted in that way? The Department of Public Works takes care of all the expenses. If there is any renting of buildings' the Department of Public Works pays for it; if there are any repairs to be done to the
buildings the Department of Public Works pays for it. If they need coal, water, light or anything like that the Department of Public Works pays for it. The minister says that they supply the paper for their own stamps. In view of that, I should like to suggest to the Postmaster General that he make a request to have the price of postage stamps reduced by at least one cent.
I explained a few minutes ago that doing that would cost the treasury $11 million, and that is just by reducing the postage one cent on first-class mail letters.
Out would go your surplus.
Yes.
That being so, would it be true to say that it would cost us $11 million.
Yes.
I think the minister said that the increase was put on for taxation purposes.
Yes.

That would reduce our revenue by $11 million. I do not think the Post Office Department is one of the most inefficiently run departments, but certainly from the financial point of view it produces less returns than any private business would consider a fair return. It has absolutely no overhead expenses, no upkeep whatever. Surely it could never be said and should not be said in the public accounts or in the estimates that the Post Office Department pays its way, because it does not. It would go in the hole if it had to pay a fair and equitable amount of expenses such as any other business is forced to do.
The hon. member will find that all departments are on the same basis. That is the system, which is followed. I do not think one can find any department that pays its light, heat, water and rent.

The hon. member knows that the Post Office Department is in an entirely different category. It is a revenue producing department; the others are not. Even if what he has said were true, which it is not, that would be no reason why the Post Office Department should carry on in such a manner.

The first
statement I made was that we do not give these figures as a profit. It is not a profit at all; it is simply an operating surplus. We

Supply-Post Office Department
are one part of the government of Canada and the public works department is there to put up buildings when necessary and to maintain them. By calculating what we should pay, we could say whether we were arriving at a surplus or not. I explained that when I began. We would arrive at a surplus of about $4 million by calculating the rental which we would pay if we were an independent business. But I have never said, and I do not wish to be understood as saying, that the $8 million is a profit. I repeat, it is not a profit at all.

I wish to come into this
discussion for a moment at this stage because of what my genial friend the hon. member for Bow River said with respect to the socialist aspect of the Post Office Department. I would indicate to the Postmaster Genera! one way whereby he could increase his revenue by over $7 million. I asked the Postmaster General a question which was answered on April 2 of this year with respect to postal matters. The answer will be found at page 1967 of Hansard. I asked certain questions with reference to second-class mail matter handled by the Post Office Department. Among other questions, I asked him what was the estimated profit or loss to the department in the handling of periodicals in the years 1944, 1945 and 1946. I was referring to newspapers and periodicals generally, and the answer I received from the department was that the loss in handling newspapers and periodicals is estimated at $7,287,400 per annum. Now out of a total budget of the Postmaster General's department this year of $67 million, the one item of handling second-class mail matter, showing an estimated loss per annum of some seven and a quarter million dollars, seems to me to be something that should be explained by the minister. Most second-class mail matter consists of newspapers which carry an extensive paid-advertising section or sections in the papers, and those sections are, particularly among the larger and bulkier periodicals, a definite source of profitable revenue to the newspapers and periodicals. It would seem to me that, instead of giving these large newspaper syndicates special concessions by way of carrying charges, so that the Canadian people, in addition to the huge advertising costs that undoubtedly are collected in the course of each year, pay the sum of $7,287,400 for carrying advertising for which the Canadian public pays in a variety of ways, the minister could improve the balance sheet of his department by placing increased charges particularly on the heavy periodicals. Those that carry a certain per 
centage of advertising should definitely pay a considerably larger amount than they are now doing for matter handled b3r the department. May I ask what the minister's policy is with respect to the tariff schedules charged for second-class mail matter? I should be pleased to have a brief statement.
It has always been the policy of the government, ever since 1882, to favour the newspapers-
I know that.

-on the
ground that it is some kind of education which is being distributed to the public. The rate has varied. In 1888 it was one cent a pound, and it became postal free. In 1899 it was one quarter of a cent a pound between the first of January and the thirtieth of June and then one-half cent a pound from the first of July, 1899. Coming to our days, it is now one cent for weeklies or monthlies published in cities with a population of 10,000, but within forty miles of those towns which are less than
10,000	the distribution is made free.
For 500 only, is it not? It is for a very limited number. I have no quarrel with that procedure. That is all right because that is local distribution.

For circulation under 10,000 copies per issue it is one cent, and over 10,000 copies per issue it is one and one-half cents. Where space is devoted to advertising the law says that fifty per cent is permissible in advertising and fifty per cent in reading matter; and, so as not to quarrel, we count from fifty-four per cent. The law says fifty per cent, and it has always been that way, but they may have advertising matter to the extent of fifty-four per cent. If they exceed fifty-four per cent and they are caught, as happens quite often, we charge them four cents a pound on all that section of the newspaper which covers advertising. I have no figures here, and I should not like to mention the newspapers that have paid fines, but some have paid heavy fines. All this is for the purpose of giving the public reading matter at a very low cost. I admit that if we charged the newspapers what the service costs the department, we would save $7,287,000. In the United States they are trying to raise the rate from three cents to four cents, and from what I read in the newspapers there is an attempt to charge the higher postal rates. But I doubt very much whether they will succeed. At all events, I would prefer to wait until they succeed before we start the same operation here.

But I see no reason why we should not precede the United States in

Supply-Post Office Department
putting our foot down on a practice which, I think, is not altogether one of share-the-wealth. The minister has given us an excellent explanation as to the historical background of how the newspapers have been expanding at the expense of the Canadian public. He might go into the matter of charging this increased rate of four cents a . pound, as I understood him to say, for the entire amount of each newspaper's advertising section. On that basis I am sure the minister would' have no difficulty in recouping the Canadian people for the seven and a quarter million dollars which we are now paying as a subsidy to the newspapers. The newspapers could not very well complain, because that portion of the newspaper is definitely extra revenue material. I do not see why the fifty per cent portion of the newspaper space is allowed to advertising and the carrying charge is made on the basis of one cenit. May I ask a further question? Is the mileage which the newspapers and periodicals are transported within Canada considered at all in his department's assessment of the carriage rate for second-class mail matter?
No, it is not. It is just like a letter.
A letter amply pays for its own weight to any portion of Canada, but second-class mail matter does not. Therefore distance should be a factor.
In any event, it is not counted.

Coming as I do from a rural, district, I should like to ask if something could not be worked out so that rural mail carriers would get a more equal salary. In my riding I know of a returned soldier who took a mail route of twenty-two miles for $825. He cannot carry it. There are other mail routes in my riding which have been put up at tender, and the tender has been too high. There is one route there paying $1,500 a year, and other routes of an equal distance are being carried for about $850. Can something not be worked out whereby these men will get a living wage? There is another man in my riding who took a route of twenty-two miles for $1,200. He told me he had $2,000 in cash out of his sale when he went in to operate that route. He operated the route for three years, and said he had spent his $2,000 and did not get a dollar out of it. So he gave up the route. I could mention the route, although the minister may know of it. It seems that these boys and old men come off the farm, go in there and think they can run these routes and make quite a big amount of money. Then they find they cannot live.
They have to get a horse or a car, and sometimes two horses. Could some fair proposition not be worked out for them so that they would get a living wage?

speechtext: Order. It appears to me that some of the discussion which has taken place tonight could more appropriately take place on the particular item concerned. For instance, .the discusion on rural mail routes could, I would think, take place on item 265, air and land mail services. Other similar discussions could more appropriately take place on the individual votes rather than on the administration item. This is a suggestion I make to the committee.

Just in that connection, may I point out that the minister himself, in opening up the discussion of the estimates this evening, brought this matter in. That is the reason it is being discussed at this time. The minister led the way and others are merely following his lead.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee not agree with me that it might be better to consider the matters as they are called by the Chair?
After this.

I think it is customary on the first item to allow considerable leeway. Probably more progress could be made in that way. I think the minister would be quite willing to answer my deskmate's question at this time. It will save its being asked later.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I might interrupt, as the hon. member for Rosedale and some others have stated, after this question is answered, does the committee not feel that we should proceed as I have suggested?

I think every other member would say that procedure should be followed after his particular question is answered. Now that this is up for fairly general discussion, I think we had better cover as much ground as we can.
There is a point I should like to draw to the minister's attention, and he might answer when, he answers my colleague. Could the post office not be a little more careful in the issuing of stamps, and have them properly centred? This is a business in Canada and in the world which our philatelists follow carefully. They have a certain pride-and it is a commendable one-in the collection of stamps of various kinds and descriptions. These stamps bring fairly high prices. For instance, the minister spoke of the Alexander Graham Bell stamp, so many of which issue

Supply-Post Office Department
were sold. This business has a material place in the revenue. I do not think Canada is any worse than any other country, but we should like to think we are a little better. I should like to see these stamps issued with a little more care. I could give the minister illustrations of my criticism right from my own- office in the House of Commons. I should like to see the stamps better centred, and better stamped. In cancelling the stamps, I should like to see the post offices throughout the country use machines which were a little more in keeping with good taste, to the end that the stamps might not be all smudged up and destroyed, as they very often are. A little care and attention on the part of the postmasters and the people who publish the stamps might very well improve the situation, and put us in a position where we could be proud of our stamps, and our philatelists would be better pleased in that regard. I would ask the minister to make a statement on that when he gives his answer to my hon. friend.
The statement is short. It has happened that stamps are spoiled. My attention has been drawn to that; I have asked my officials to see to it and given instructions that they be more careful.

I do not think the matter raised by the hon. member for Regina should be allowed to drop. Anybody who makes a suggestion for the saving of $7,000,000 to the Canadian taxpayers has really got something. We ought to enlist the services of the best minds we have around here and get them working on it. Every time I think of the difficulty we have in establishing mail services in small towns-I understand the minister has financial problems, and I can appreciate them-I realize that this $7,000,000 would go a great distance in helping out many of the members here with regard to the postal problems in their ridings. When I think of our dragging carloads of these Toronto Weekly Stars-and we will just take that as an example; I imagine that is the worst offender-
Try the Globe and Mail.

We are dragging carloads of these newspapers over the mountains, and I imagine the department is absorbing that mountain differential about which so much has been said in British Columbia. When one thinks of the educational features of that paper, what does he find? The bulk of the weekly edition consists of Orphan Annie, Dagwood and various fantastic articles on what science might do one hundred years from now.
The hon. member must be a careful reader of that paper.

As a matter of fact, I avoid it assiduously; I can assure the hon. member of that. But we do not get enough revenue out of that newspaper to pay for its delivery after its gets to Vancouver, let alone to pay the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National what they must ' charge for taking it over there. We are having great difficulty in British Columbia in obtaining sufficient newsprint to publish newspapers large enough to contain all the news we have to print; yet we see these thick newspapers brought in from Ontario at the expense of the taxpayers. I think it is about time we quit subsidizing these newspaper millionaires in Canada. It may have been an excellent plan in 1882, before we had the radio, but I believe we in western Canada could certainly do without a great deal of the type of literature that is shipped the longest distance at the least expense. If I never see the Star out there I can get along very well.

Item agreed to.
262. Post offices, including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices, $30,838,101.

How much was collected last year in overdue postage? If one receives mail from the United States it may lack one cent; one has to pay two cents, and there always has to be someone at home to pay the postage, otherwise the postman does not deliver it.
We do not keep track of that. I suppose the hon. gentleman is speaking of postcards with something written on them, which may come in with only a one-cent stamp?
Would that require three cents or two cents, coming from the United States? What is the rate from the United States to Canada on postcards?
One cent.
And if anything is written on the postcard it is three cents?
Correct.
From the United States to Canada?
Yes.

But there are no records showing how much was collected in overdue postage? I imagine it would be a small amount, and I suggest that probably it costs the Post Office Department more to collect

Supply-Post Office Department
it than it is worth. I do not think any substantial amount of mail would be sent purposely with less than the required postage.

It is a comparatively small amount. Of course the United States also collects for us whenever a letter is loaded too heavily, for example. We receive the letter and give instructions on it to collect so much and that amount is collected in the United States. We collect when they give us instructions to do so, but we do not keep a special account for that. As I think the insurance companies say, it Is knock for knock.
This matter of overdue postage-
It is a very small amount.
I would expect it to be, but it is a great nuisance to people, and I think it comes about through inadvertence rather than intent.
But if we did not collect it, and that became known, it might become a custom.

One might think it would become a custom if it were known that the post office would not collect overdue postage, but I point out that if one wished to do so, where letters are sent out by the thousand one could ship them over to the United States and use the United States three-cent rate as against the Canadian four-cent rate, if I followed the minister a moment ago. People do not do those things, however; it is not worth while. If the Post. Office Department delivered this underpaid mail, particularly and perhaps exclusively when it comes from another postal jurisdiction, without collecting the extra charge, I do not think they would lose anything. I am sure the cost of collection must be greater than the amount collected, without considering the inconvenience to the people, because, as I said, they cannot get their mail unless they happen to be at home to give the postman the two cents, or whatever the amount may be. Then the postman has to write that down on a form and I suppose that form has to be audited. So, if the Post Office Department had records showing the cost of collection I believe they would find they were actually out of pocket. I would! suggest that the Postmaster General give this freedom of postage, if I might use that term, a trial; then if he found it abused he might have to revert to the old system.

I must tell the hon. gentleman this is one of the obligations imposed under the contract with the postal union. It is done all over the world.
Mr. JACKMAN; All I can ask, then, is that the Postmaster General use his good influence when he attends the next international convention.

Would the minister answer my question, please, in regard to rural mail carriers?
The CHAIRMAN; Order. Would the committee carry item 262 first?
No. I want to ask a question on it.

I will answer the question first. There are not many items in my department; as the hon. member for Lake Centre said, I was probably the first offender because I wanted to give an over-all picture of the department, and then the discussion continued.
As to the question asked by the hon. gentleman, these tenders are called from a certain class of people, who perhaps are not chartered accountants. By that I mean they did not have the chance to go to college. This is the tender principle, and it is unfortunate when these tenders come in too low. We do not like that, as a matter of fact; but the law obliges us to accept the lowest tender, and if we do not do that we fall into difficulties. For that reason we have varied the contracts to give these tenderers a chance after three months' notice to get out of their contracts, if they so desire. But that is the principle in force in all departments, except that the contracts given by the Post Office Department are for smaller amounts. As I said when we passed the act in regard to supplements, I had a bill prepared this year to increase the amount of a contract the Postmaster General may give without asking for tenders. That amount should be around $1,000, but it is only $200 today. The bill I had prepared put the figure at $500; but I withdrew that bill, and I do not know whether I shall bring it in another year. Such legislation would be some kind of protection to these people. At the same time, of course, it might give someone an opportunity to favour a man of his own party, whoever might be in office. I would not do that, of course; but it is a possibility, and for that reason we have been asking for tenders.

When the estimates were up a year ago I brought to the attention of the minister the fact that postal foremen of letter carriers in substations had not been given the advance they had been promised.

Supply-Post Office Department
Have the salaries of postal foremen in substations been advanced to what they should be?
I am told they have now been adjusted. First, we adjusted the rank and file, and now they have all been adjusted.	.
What is the rate now?
If the hon. member would give us a position, for example, we would be able to give him the information more quickly.
Take any of the branch post offices in Toronto; station "L" for example.

I can get
the information and give it to the hon. member privately. But I can give my word we have adjusted them all.

In a number of the
branch post offices in Toronto the letters are sorted in the basement.
At Christmas time that has to be done, because of pressure of work.

I am not finding fault;
the basements I have been in are quite satisfactory. But in the summer months they are extremely warm on account of lack of ventilation. Has the department considered putting in fans?

I shall take
a note of that, and make representations to the Department of Public Works.
I understand that class "B" post office employees are not civil servants; is that correct?

They are
not. We have revenue postmasters who are paid so much out of revenue, and are not civil service employees. They do not pay anything for superannuation, and do not receive pensions when they leave their positions. Their employees are paid by the postmasters of those offices. Then, in class "2B" the postmaster is a civil servant, but his employees are not. The department fixes the rate at which they are to be paid.

Last winter the starting wage was $87 a month for new employees. The town of Lloydminster in my constituency is growing rapidly, and at the present time is experiencing an oil boom. At that point the postmaster has found it impossible to get help at .$87 a month. Those workers in the post office, along, with the postmaster, are working fifty-two hours a week. I have taken fMr. MacNicol.]
the matter up with the deputy minister, but I do not know whether any change has been made.
I am informed that he has those representations on his desk, and that he is looking into the matter.

Are the salaries received
by postal clerks the same in all offices? For instance, are they the same in the Charlottetown and Toronto offices? Is a man doing the same work and putting in the same hours in those respective offices paid on the same basis?

The postal
clerks in the small cities do not reach the same maximum as those in large cities such as Toronto, because they do not have as much work.

The}'' are doing the same
work and putting in the same hours.
No, the work is not as difficult. To sort mail in the larger cities they have to pass examinations, and it is much more difficult.

I understand that the
minister's department has received certain recommendations with reference to the post office at Sussex, New Brunswick. What changes or alterations have been recommended? In my opinion there should also be a new post office building in that town. The present one was built in 1889, when Sir George Foster represented the constituency. The population has increased from less than 1,000 to nearly 4,000.

We are
making a change in that post office. I am told there is an item in the public wmrks estimates for that.
The item has been recommended by the Post Office Department?

Yes, we are
making changes there. I understand that a staircase is to be built on the outside.

What changes have been
recommended?

I shall write
the hon. member to tell him that.

I understand that there are some smaller post offices the revenue of which is determined by the amount of postage stamps they sell. Mail delivery is given at those offices. I have in mind the post office at Woodroffe. just outside the city of Ottawa, where mail delivery is given, but where the revenue to the postmaster is not sufficient to permit his giving a proper service and having

Supply-Post Office Department
a regular establishment. Could the Postmaster General do something for such post offices which would enable the postmaster to give efficient service to the people in the community who want their mail delivered, but who are working in the city of Ottawa, for instance, and do not buy postage stamps or register their mail at that office, and in this way do not contribute to its revenue, or to the revenues which would normally come to a post office?
When answering that, would the minister give some information respecting the requirements of the Post Office Department as to the number of people in an area where mail delivery will be given? We know that street conditions, the numbering of streets and matters of that kind are considered. However I know of some areas where mail delivery is given and other areas more congested where it is not given. What is the yardstick used by the Post Office Department in deciding which areas shall get delivery and which shall not?

With respect to the first question, the people who receive their mail at a post office are supposed to buy their stamps there. The hon. member will realize, however, how difficult it would be to enforce that expectation, particularly in view of the fact that people will buy their stamps in the city when they are coming to the city each day. They do not save anything by so doing, and perhaps they cheat the postmaster at the office where they get their mail. They drop their letters in the boxes in the city.
If in his question the hon. member is referring to the giving of a letter carrier service to a small town immediately adjacent to Ottawa, for example, the reply would be that we do not need 2,000 points of call because we would simply be extending the service given in the larger Ottawa area. To give a direct answer, I would have to have a survey made of the area in question.

Perhaps I can put my .question more clearly. An extension was given recently to a certain street in my constituency. It happens that two streets farther on there are more residents requiring the service. I believe they merit that service, but the extension was not made far enough to include those two streets where the population is more congested than it is in the area in which it was given.
We will look into that.

I have been speaking about mail delivery at McKellar, which is not in
Ottawa, and also mail delivery in Ottawa West and in Westboro south of the railway tracks, noth of which areas are deserving of service.
I will look into the matter.
What has been the net increase in the number of employees of the Post Office Department appointed by the civil service commission since May 1, 1945?
Does the hon. member mean the increase in money?
No, the increase in numbers.

I have no comparative figures as far back as that but we could furnish them later. I have comparative figures for 1946 and 1947. For departmental administration as of April 1, 1946, we had 118 permanent and 56 temporary employees, or a total of 174. As of April 1, 1947, we had 102 permanent and 73 temporary employees, or a total of 175. The grand total for post office headquarters administration, inspectors, railway mail service, air and land mail service was, as of April 1, 1946, 662 permanent and 520 temporary employees, or a total of 1,182. As of April 1, 1947, there were 592 permanent and 557 temporary employees, a total of 1,149 as against 1,182 the previous year. So that there was a small reduction here at headquarters.
I have also the number of employees in staff post, offices, in district offices and in the railway mail service as of the dates indicated. As of July 31, 1945, the grand total of employees was 13,196, an increase of 1,597. As of May 31, 1946, the grand total of employees was 14,293, an increase of 1,097. As of February 28, 1947, the grand total was 14,678, an increase of 385. The number of temporaries had increased on that date by 848, and there was a decrease of 463 in the permanent employees. We are making temporaries permanent as we go along.

These figures do not very well fit in with an answer which the minister gave me the other day in sessional paper No. 106N, in answer to the question:
How many appointments to permanent or temporary positions with salaries per annum
(a)	under $2,000;	(b) between $2,000 and
$3,000; (e) over $3,000, have been made to the civil service since May 9, 1945?
The answer so far as the Post Office Department was concerned was (a) permanent 57, temporary 6,129; (b) permanent 19, temporary 1.
It is pointed out in this return that this does not include postmasters whose remuneration is based on the revenue of their offices. This reply would indicate an increase of some

Supply-Post Office Department
6,000	employees, permanent and temporary, during a period of two years. That is tlhe reason I asked my question, because it appeared to me that either a mistake is made in this return or a substantial error has been made by the minister in the answer he has given to the committee.
If the answer the hon. gentleman has quoted is for the post office, there is a big error there.

That is why I asked that question as to how many appointments to temporary and permanent positions had been made in the past two years and what had been the increase in the two years. I wish the minister would procure that information, because this return would indicate a phenomenal increase in the number of employees during the past two years.
The next question I wanted to ask the minister is this. In this return I asked whether or not the veterans preference was being followed in making appointments to the civil service. I wish to ask the minister that question as to his department. Is the veterans preference being lived up to?

Definitely.
Almost every day we are replacing temporary employees who have been there for years, some of them for five years, with veterans.

I appreciate that answer from the minister, because from this return the indication is that in some other departments there is a serious departure from the veterans preference, since it sets forth in detail the numbers who have been appointed to the civil service in that period of two years and shows that 11,094 males who were not entitled to the veterans preference were appointed to the civil service in a period of two years. That indicates a substantial departure from the veterans preference. Could the minister indicate what precentage of the 6,000 odd appointments made to the Post Office Department in the past two years have been of those entitled to the veterans preference?

Those are civilian employees. Those who qualified) by examination, 1,080; those not qualified 267; those who are married women, 21, or a total of 1,368 civilians as against 5,044 returned employees entitled to veterans preference.
In the event that there is a vacancy in the rural post office, is the preference given to the veteran??
Yes, every time that a veteran falls within the regulation-he has to live for twelve months in the place of work, for example-we give him the preference.
There is no departure from that?

No. There might be a departure if the man is found not fit to fill the job. For example, today I received a complaint on moral grounds about the preference that had been given. We have not yet decided on the question. We have asked those who made the complaints to furnish us with the proof. If it is found that the complaint is true we shall have to withdraw the appointment, but only if it is proved beyond the shadow of a doubt.

I should like to ask a question for the purpose of information. When I was in Vancouver a little while ago it was drawn to my attention that many businesses were installing stamping machines, or at least a system of providing their own stamps so that stamps were not bought at the local post offices. That curtails the revenue which goes to the small post office. When letter stamping machines, or whatever the technical name is, are installed in a plant or a factory or a store or something of that kind, in a small community in a city served by a sub-post office, is the revenue from that

Supply-Post Office Department
machine credited to the sub-post office or to the central post office in. the city?
It is credited to the central post office. A sub-post office does not handle the mail. When the subpost office is a small office we pay a minimum.

That is quite true, but the postmaster in this post office where I do the little business I have to do told me that within recent times-as the minister knows, in every city there are small business communities which are easily served by a sub-post office-several large buyers of stamps and post office money orders and so forth-my question would apply only to stamps-have put in stamping machines and he was deprived of this business. Consequently his remuneration was much less than it formerly was and otherwise would be if the machines were not installed. I was wondering whether some method could be employed so that in a given area the business that the sub-post office would have received had the machines not been installed could be credited to the sub-post office.

If the subpost office handles the mail of the big company which has the meters-we call them meters; they pass their mail through the meters which are checked by the officials- they would get consideration. But usually these letters are not handled by the sub-post offices. The mail goes in the bag and then to the main post office. If they were handled by the sub-postmaster he would have the right to have the revenue from them.

Some time ago the minister said that he was filing answers to questions. Probably the question I am about to ask has already been answered. I am speaking of conditions in the town of Trenton where in 1945 letter delivery in the town was first requested, The revenue was then over 840,000. Trenton is known as a town with the population of a city, over 10,000. There are more residents on the east side of the Trent river than on the west side. They have to walk across a long bridge to get to the post office which is on the west side of the town. What is the situation with regard to the application for letter delivery in the town of Trenton?
I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to the establishing of sub-post offices. During the war a request was made to establish a sub-post office in an area outside the city of Belleville. This area is quite densely populated and known as College Hill. Through that area there is a single rural mail route travelled. These people are quite a distance from the post office and are anxious
to know how they can be served with a daily mail service.
My officers are going to get the answers because figures are involved. I shall give the answer in a little while.

The post office in every rural community is usually considered as the embodiment of" the federal government. It is about the only connection these people have with the federal administration. My remarks on this item might very well have been directed to the Minister of Public Works when his estimates were before the committee. Post offices have been, as one hon. member suggested tonight, more or less the neglected children in the last six or eight years. Owing to the war we had to curtail our expenditure in building; in many parts of Canada we have post offices not exactly what they should be, and in many other parts of the country we have a real need for new post office buildings. As I understand it, the Department of Public Works has decided that post offices might be built in cities where the revenue was over $10,000. I believe that this figure might be regarded as more or less an arbitrary one, because we have many progressive little communities where the post office may not have that revenue and where there is real need for buildings for federal services and especially post offices. I am told that whenever the department or the Postmaster General makes such recommendations to the public works department they are given special consideration, but yet we are tied up by the over-all rule. I wish that consideration were given to small centres. I have in my constituency a point where in 1939 the Postmaster General's department recommended1 the construction of a post office. It was approved by the public works department and the contract signed, but the contractor, for reasons of his own, did not start work right away. The fall came and it was too late for him to start building the post office. Early in 1940, owing to the recommendations of the Minister of Finance, those contracts which had not yet been started, in respect of buildings not yet being erected, had to be stopped. I wish the department would take into consideration as early as possible the advisability of providing more post office buildings in the small progressive centres throughout the country.

As I said a few minutes ago, we hope to be able next year to build quite a number, and those already started will be given immediate consideration.
As to the question asked about Trenton, that is a great prospective office. The revenue

Supply-Post Office Department
for 1945-46 was $54,344, and the number of householder points of call, 2,020. According to these figures, the city does qualify for letter carriers. There may be something else, but if the hon. gentleman wishes us to make a thorough examination and give an answer in writing we shall do so.

In prosecuting this matter in 1946, some officials of the department said to me, "Your revenue is up in the required brackets, but remember that Trenton was a war-boom town. Where will you be next year?" I assured them that we were on safe ground, and the figures quoted by the minister bear me out, because it was ten thousand higher than it was in the last year of the war. I thank the minister for the consideration.

May I ask the minister a question along the lines of some asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre. The question is this: In the case of the establishment of sub-post offices, or a change in or the appointment of a postmaster to a sub-post office, is the veteran always given the preference?

In a sub-post office, as the hon. member will realize, location is the main thing and we grant sub-post offices mainly on the basis of locations so as to serve the surrounding district. It did happen in Montreal, however, that the man in a sub-post office died and another man bought the trade and wanted to have the sub-post office. Before granting the request, however, we advertised through the Legion to see whether in the surrounding district there were veterans who wished to have it. We are expecting an answer before we grant it. We favour the veterans wherever we can.

I am glad to hear that. I do not know whether the minister is aware of the conditions in Saint John but I would appreciate it if he would let me know why a veteran named Gray, a young man in the city of Saint John, did not receive the appointment and was not put in charge of a sub-post office, as had been promised.
When was that?
Within the last six months.
I will inquire and write to the hon. gentleman.
I should like to get an answer.

Following up the remarks of the hon. member for Bellechasse regarding some of the smaller centres, I may say that there is a progressive town in my constituency at Pine Falls, where approximately $2 million is to be spent this coming year. The post

office which is there now is just an old shack which possibly was built when the town had a population of about two hundred. There is now a population of over two thousand. In view of the fact that this is a progressive little town and that a good deal of money is being spent there, I hope the Postmaster General will take into consideration the building of a new post office there this coming year.
I will make a note of the hon. gentleman's remarks.

Item agreed to.
265. Air and land mail services, $17,028,943.

On the first item tonight I asked the minister whether we would get a delivery service in Swift Current this year. I asked the question then so as to give him an opportunity to cogitate, to think the matter over. I am sure Swift Current has met the required conditions. I asked him to give me some assurance or otherwise-it would not take long-as to whether we shall get that service. I would ask him now to give me an answer, even if it is only a brief yes or no.

If the hon. gentleman wishes to believe me, I will do the utmost to give him service, and he will probably know very soon, that is, when the supple-mentaries come down.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, as regards the closing of post offices on Sunday, I understand it was ordered following requests made throughout the country, first by those whose duty it is to see that the Lord's Day is observed, and in the second place by postmasters. Despite the requests from those twm quartern, which, I understand, have compelled the minister to take such a decision, perhaps irrevocably, notwithstanding a tradition which went back to the time when the department came inito being, would it not be possible to leave at least some discretion to those postmasters who wish to keep their offices open at least for one hour on Sunday after mass, for the benefit of people who live far away and who are unable to call for their mail except on Sunday. I believe the department could avoid the expense which such closing entails, through subsequent requests for the establishment of a rural mail service.

As the hon. member knows, that matter was decided upon when I became Postmaster General. We are often requested to reopen the post offices on Sunday. After considering the matter seriously, we came to the conclusion that in some

Supply-Post Office Department
localities it would have been preferable to keep the post office open, since there was no rural mail service. We are now reconsidering the matter.
(Text):

The minister has been most genial toward hon. members with regard to the consideration of requests for various things. I should like to speak for a group in western Canada who have been trying for many years to have more rural routes established there. In travelling through the three western provinces, one is surprised at the small number of rural routes. I do not believe that over ten to fifteen per cent of our rural population is so served, while in eastern Canada I am sure that ninety per cent of the rural population is served by rural routes. Not only that, but on a number of our western routes, and, I believe, on the majority of them, mail deliveries are made only twice a week. If the minister has the figures, I should like him to give the number of rural routes in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, the number of applications which have been made for rural routes in those provinces during the last year and the number that he has been able to grant.

I must say that we have these figures, but I have not them here. I admit that the western provinces are not served by rural mail delivery as well as some other provinces, and we intend to do something to correct that situation.
I hope the minister does. I know, of course, there are greater difficulties out there.
Expenses are higher.

Yes; the distances are greater. But with the better roads out there now, a great many of these routes should be established in the near future. Last year the minister gave a break-down of the cost of mailing parcels to Great Britain and to Europe, as between the amount which the Canadian post office received, the amount which the shipping companies received and the amount which went to the post office in the country of delivery. At that time I was very much surprised to see the proportion of the dollar spent in postage which went to the shipping companies. The minister stated that was because of the high rates which had been placed on shipping during the war, and that new contracts were being negotiated. How far has the minister progressed in negotiating these new contracts? Can he give the committee a break-down of those costs today as compared with a year ago?
I do not remember that I said the war was responsible for the high price charged by the company.
Well, insurance rates.

It is true that it cost us that. Although the amount paid by the Canadian mailer of a parcel seems to be high, very little stays in Canada. I remember that on a parcel of eleven pounds, for example, there was only thirty-seven cents which stayed in Canada. England was taking around fifty-five or fifty-nine cents for delivering that parcel to a point a short distance away from Liverpool. We were taking thirty-seven cents to take the parcel in Vancouver and bring it to Halifax. Then the company was taking so much, according to*the cubic content and the size of the parcel of eleven pounds. On a parcel of twenty pounds it was a little different. It is difficult to ask the English postal authorities to reduce their rates. They reduced them early this year and we have passed that reduction on to the Canadian shipper.
I realize that, but it seemed to me that the shipping companies were getting the larger share of the amount payable.

We have
taken that up with the companies and they have refused to make any reduction.

Does the department
know whether it is making or losing money on postal notes and money orders?
According to my officials, we are just about breaking even.

Some years ago I understood that there was a flat percentage rate on these money orders, and that it was found that for the small amounts people would use the post office, while for the larger amounts, where there was a sliding scale in effect, the people would use private companies such as the express companies, I suppose. As a result, I understand that the post office changed its rate on money orders, so that in place of a flat percentage rate, there was a sliding scale. The buyer paid a lower percentage if he bought a large amount, and therefore the post office competed on a fairer basis with the private companies. May I ask what the result of that was? Did it take place? I am informed by a good source, namely, the previous postmaster general, that it did.

The acting deputy minister says that he does not remem-
Supply-Post Office Department

ber that, and he has been here for forty years. Perhaps the hon. member wants to talk about the parcel post as compared with the express post.
No. I understand that it is with regard to money orders.
I have been Postmaster General for only two years. I am told it was never on a percentage basis.
I understand that Trans-Canada Air Lines is going to arrange for a stop at the airport at Swift Current. Will that automatically give Swift Current air mail service?

Yes.
(Translation):

Am I to understand, Mr. Chairman, that the erection of post office buildings in various localities depends on two considerations, which are that the revenue must be above $10,000, and the population must exceed 10,000? This means that the department will not erect post office buiidings in rural constituencies where the revenue is less than $10,000, before having provided for such buildings in the larger centres of this country?

Mr. Chairman, there is no hard and fast rule. However, we have to consider first the larger centres, but we hope to be able to give a chance to various constituencies where the population is not very large.
Will our chance come some time during the present fiscal year, or shall we have to wait till doomsday?

Next year.

I want to make a recommendation to the minister at this time. It is with reference to a class of post office employees or workers who were mentioned once before tonight, and who have been mentioned, I expect, many times in debate, and who, it seems to me, are out of luck. I refer to those who are paid according to the revenue which the post office takes in; I think they get a percentage of last year's stamp sales, besides what they get this year. In some of these smaller places the postmaster is required 
to be on the job all day long and is prevented from having any side line; still he is not paid enough to be able to put very much away. Until eleven o'clock last evening we were discussing other ways of taking care of such people, and it was generally admitted that the method being discussed in that debate was not quite enough to bring up the incomes of these people to whatever the maximum may be according to their marital status. So that I believe the postal authorities and the government generally should be giving some consideration to a scheme under which these people will be given a retiring allowance. I know one postmaster who is a little over eighty years of age. He would like to retire, but he cannot very well live on what he would get as an old age pension, certainly not on what it has been up to the present; and in the past his earnings have not been great enough to permit him to save anything for his old age. I wish the minister would give some consideration to this matter.
I must tell the hon. gentleman that this question is at present being studied in the department.
Then try to get that study culminated before this old chap dies, will you?
Item agreed to.
S58. General administration, $273,043.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the minister to whom the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is now responsible, I cannot but appreciate the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat; and the applause with which they were received indicates that he was merely expressing the sentiments of the committee.
I should like to answer some of the specific questions asked by the hon. gentleman, because it seems to me that the answers are absolutely conclusive. His first objection or complaint was that promotions were held up for too long. The proportion of non-commissioned officers to constables is higher than it has ever been before in the history of the force; there is one non-commissioned officer to every constable. In the administration of
a force, one cannot simply go on promoting for the sake of meeting the personal requirements of the constables, if you overload the force completely with those who are not constables. That is the reason promotions cannot be made faster than they are being made at the present time.
Could that be covered by adding to the amount paid after a certain period of time and making the increment equivalent to that in non-commissioned ranks?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question of pay is another thing. The pay of the force must be kept in line, or should be kept in line with what is fair for police forces in the country. I think that is the only responsible way to look at the matter. When my hon. friend talks about the pay of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police being low he should take into consideration the other privileges which members of that force have in addition to pay, including such matters as pension privileges, and the like. One cannot simply segregate the per diem wages or remuneration of the members of a force, unless he also takes into account the other numerous and valuable privileges the members of that force have.

Are there first and
second-class constables?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, there are first, second and third-class constables.
With varying pay rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, with varying pay rates. And there are corporals, sergeants and staff sergeants. Without having studied the matter, I should think that to put the pay purely on a basis of time served, instead of upon rank attained, would be a bad organization of a force. I do not believe it would be done; and I am speaking without having considered the question from all angles. But it would seem to me that, in business or in any other organization, the mere putting in of a certain number of months or years should not be the only requirement for a raise in pay. The important thing is that the pay should be adjusted to the rank.
Then the hon. member raised the point about the marriage regulations. This afternoon the commissioner told me that eighty-three per cent of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are married. I ask him what he considered would be a reasonable proportion of a police force to be married. Hon. members. must bear in mind that it would be out of the question to have a police force were too many were married, because the obstacles in
4812	COMMONS
Supply-Royal Canadian Mounted Police
connection, with mobility which arise from a state of affairs like that are most serious. At the present time there is difficulty in getting thirty-four men for the northern service because of the unwillingness of the married men to go on missions of that kind. There are the further difficulties of moving their families and taking children out of school. There ought to be a substantial proportion of the force who are single. The commissioner told me today that perhaps a proportion of thirty per cent single men would be a reasonable one. Many police forces have a much higher proportion than that. However, in this force only seventeen per cent are single. Therefore there must be these marriage regulations. That is the reason for them.
In organizing and administering a force of this kind, one can be ever so sympathetic to the personal requirements or desires of the members of the force, but there are overriding considerations in the public interest which have to be served.
What are the rates of pay of the various classes of constables, noncommissioned officers and1 officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The pay of first-class constables is $3.25 a day to $3.50 a day, or per annum it is $1,186.25 to $1,277.50. The pay of second-class constables is $3 a day, or $1,095 per annum, and of third-class constables it is $2.75 a day, or $1,003.75 per annum. In addition to that, there are allowances. Officers living out of quarters may be granted a genera! living allowance not exceeding $4 a day, or $1,460 a year. Non-commissioned officers and constables living out of quarters may be granted a general living allowance at the following rates: married, $2.25 a day or $821.25 per annum; single, $1.50 a day, or $547.50 per annum.

I should like to say a word on the point raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I believe that some day we shall have to face the issue in an all-embracing way. We have to concede today that it is not the individual or the ability that receives the high salary. It is the position. Having made the position, we apply the salary to it. Then, if a promotion is made the individual gets the salary.
Let us take the cases of constables A and B who joined the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We will assume they both have similar qualifications and similar devotion to duty. They have served their apprenticeship, or whatever the term is, in the first, second and third classes. Then a promotion is to be made. Constable A is chosen for the position, and [Mr. Ilsley.l
receives the salary and other advantages going with it. Constable B has to remain in the force, unless he wishes to get out, although he has the same qualifications and the same devotion to duty as constable A has.
When the question of pension comes up, the pensions are usually based on the salary received. So that any justice or fairness is purely arbitrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid I do not understand the hon. member.
Perhaps not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is taking a hypothetical case of two men of exactly equal ability and devotion to duty.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is only one position open. One is taken and the other is not.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Are there ever two men of exactly equal ability and devotion to duty? In an examination, is it not always the case of someone exercising his discretion to select the better of two men to discharge the position?
Even if there is an examination, I do not believe an examination can ever give a true indication of an individual's ability.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Possibly the judgment of his superior can.

Even the judgment of his superiors may be wrong, and the man with lesser ability may be appointed. It is the same way with the selection of judges. So many factors enter into the selection, intangibles that depend upon the likes and dislikes of those making the appointment. I am not finding fault with the minister or his department. I am merely showing that our arrangements in the matter are purely arbitrary and, in their operation, quite discriminatory. They do not do fairness as between individuals or groups. I am satisfied that if we are to have a well ordered society we shall have to find some way by which we can put people on a more equal basis than is achieved by these arbitrary decisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I usually agree with my hon. friend in most of the things he says in this house, but I do not think he has made a case against anything but human nature in his argument tonight.

Far be it from me to try to make a case against human nature. But human nature is not a static thing. Human

Royal Canadian Mounted Police
nature reacts according to its environment. In one environment the same individual reacts one way, and in another environment he reacts another way. I am not finding fault with the minister. I am merely trying to show the flaws in our ways of doing things. A place of rank and position carries with it implications that give the children and grandchildren of the individual occupying that position certain advantages which other people have not, regardless of their ability or their service to the community. When the minister gets more time to think over what I have said I am sure he will agree with me.

Might I suggest that
there is no service in which luck plays a greater part than it does in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. For instance, two constables go out to two different detachments. A crime is committed in one of these detachments and no crime is committed in the other. The constable who has had several crimes committed in his detachment is, of course, brought to the notice of his superior officers, whereas the other poor man merely puts in his weekly and monthly reports. While he does his work conscientiously, he does not enjoy the same opportunities which the constable had whose good fortune it was to be in a detachment where a certain amount of crime was committed.
Might I ask how many constables and non-commissioned officers have been promoted to commissioned rank during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Nine non-commissioned
officers have been promoted to be commissioned officers during the past year.

What are the qualifications
for entering the force? Are they higher or lower than pre-war? I have a particular reason for asking, because I have been led to believe that the qualifications have been lowered. That may not be true. Have the qualifications been lowered physically or from the point of view of scholastic attainments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are the same now as
before the war.

They have never been
changed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, but there was a period
when they were lowered.
But not now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

I cannot refrain from rising to make one comment on the remarks of the hon. member 83166-307
for Vancouver Bast. Like the minister, I find myself in agreement with the hon. member often, sometimes more often than I should like to admit. But tonight I suggest that the minister has given a complete answer by saying that what the hon. member is complaining against is human nature. At the end of his speech I could not see that we got anywhere except that either we should promote nobody or we should promote everybody.

I think the statement
of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario leaves a little to be desired. I can see the minister's point of view and the difficulties that his officials would have in trying to administer things to suit all human beings in the force or out of it. But I believe one thing that can be given consideration is this. After all, the elements of luck and ability have entered into the active service of the constable. When the time for his retirement or superannuation comes, one thing about human nature that is pretty generally true of all people is that they all need the same to live on. Suppose a man has served well and honourably as a constable and perhaps, through that element of luck which the hon. member for Nanaimo mentioned, has gained a substantial promotion because he was fortunate enough to be in a detachment where crime was committed, and that another man lias given good service, done a good job but did not have that chance of promotion. Nevertheless, when the latter retires he needs just as much to live on as the other fellow that got promoted. So why should their superannuation not be equalized upon their retiremenlt from the force? .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Upwards, I suppose?
If one man requires 1500 or $200 or $100 a month to live on when he retires, so does the other man. Equalizes it upwards or downwards whichever you like.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman apply that principle to the superannuation of the civil service?
I would apply it to every single individual in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman would equalize all pensions?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And equalize all incomes, too?

Not necessarily, because when people are drawing an income they are earning. When they retire they get a retire-



Royal Canadian Mounted Police
ment allowance and are not earning any more. But they need the same amount of money to live on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Do they not require the same amount of income to live on before they retire?
Mr. BENTLEY": Certainly they do, but I do not think the minister would consider that. My statement can stand. I will not argue further with the minister.

I should like to remind the hon. member for Vancouver East that human nature as he suggests does change, and there is a modern school of psychology, of which I am not a strong supporter, which teaches that people should work for the glory of the work itself and not for the reward that is in it.
I wish to ask the minister about a matter which grieved me very much one year when the estimates of the department were before us. It had to do with men in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who resigned from the force in order to join His Majesty's forces and take up arms overseas. When they were demobilized some of them were taken back on the strength of the force, and they found that this marriage bar of five years had to be served anew, or perhaps the time they had served with the force before going on active service overseas was taken into account too. In any event, the time during which they served in the armed services did not count in the five years. What I should like to ask is: How many men who were in the R.C.M.P. before the war resigned, and after active service are again members of the R.C.M.P. and are single? The minister knows what I am getting at. If there is an easier way to answer it, it will suit me just as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Ninety-eight have come
back to the force. I have not the figures as to whether they are single or how many are single.

We have a different minister in charge of this department now, and I wonder whether he would give consideration to the fact that the discipline of the force in the eyes of the chief of it required that men stay in the R.C.M.P. rather than resign, as I understood it, to enlist in the active service. It was what I would term iron discipline. It may have been necessary; but it seems to me that if discipline as strong as that is to be exercised, then one does not deserve very much credit for the result. Will the minister give consideration to the fact that men did not get permission to have leave of absence to go

on active service, resigned to enter the armed services and have come back? Will he give consideration to their being permitted to count the time when they were on active service as part of their five-year marriage limitation?
Mr. ILSLEY": I will discuss that matter with the commissioner.

Will the minister give the present strength of the force, its distribution, and whether or not the present strength is greater now than it was in 1946?
Mr. ILSLEY":	The present uniformed
strength of the force is 2,490. The second question was whether it had increased during the past year and by how much?

Or decreased?
Mr. ILSLEY': There has been an increase of roughly 500 during the past year.

On this item I should like to say a few words. I do not see any other item more appropriate than this one on which to make these remarks. I think I should say a few words of commendation on a certain activity which the mounted police are giving to my personal knowledge. I refer to the courses they are giving by having a constable and various officers speak to the youth of our community, explaining to them the relationship of the police to the public at large. During the last year or so, and particularly during the celebration of the citizenship presentation and explanation, I have had the experience of having a member of the mounted police talk to the youth in the various schools and explain to them the relationship of the police to public maintenance of justice and order and in that way gain the confidence of the youth in the mounted police. It is my frank opinion that one of the greatest things to foster a proper understanding of the administration of justice and confidence in the law of the land is a thorough understanding by our youth of the role of the police in the community, and to understand that the policeman is the protector and the friend of their rights.
On several occasions I have listened to a lecture given by one of the mounted police, and I refer to him particularly, although I believe others deserve commendation as well. I refer to Corporal Ade of this community, who has gone from place to place explaining to the youth the role of the police in the community. I believe that the educational work of the R.C.M.P., who are held in great esteem by the youth of our country, is of the highest order. Having been interested in that

United Nations
work, I took the liberty of asking the mounted police to give me particulars of their programme in that regard and was very glad to receive it. I studied it thoroughly. I say to the Minister of Justice that this work can be carried on extensively to the benefit of our community, and it is one of the best ways of maintaining a law-abiding state and having our youth understand that the policeman is a friend and not an enemy; that justice is something to be sought for, not something to be despised. I say to the commissioner and to the Minister of Justice the people of Canada owe a debt of gratitude to the R.C.M.P. for their action in that regard. I would ask the minister to lend all the encouragement, that he can to that particular work.
A member of this group would like to say something on this item. I would ask the minister if he will allow it to stand, although I will not press the request.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All right.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, June 30, 1947
